slides.topic: Chromosomal Abnormalities I — Karyotypes & Numerical Disorders — source 24
slides.text:
Types of Genetic Diseases
Chromosome disorders - Changes in the number or structure of chromosomes.

Single-gene disorders (MONOgenic) - single genes are changed (These are mendelian conditions) 

Multifactorial (Complex) disorders (POLYgenic)- multiple gene combinations changed sometimes with environmental causes.

Mitochondrial disorders - caused by changes in the small cytoplasmic mitochondrial chromosome.

24
Cytogenetics: The study of chromosomes and their abnormalities

slides.topic: Chromosomal Abnormalities I — Karyotypes & Numerical Disorders — source 25
slides.text:
Why do Chromosomal Disorders happen?
Causes - Ionising radiation, viral infections and chemical toxin.

Chromosome disorders - Changes in the number or structure of chromosomes.
Aneuploidy - Abnormal number of chromosomes in a cell.
Monosomy - One LESS copy of a chromosome pair. Instead of the usual 46 chromosomes, monosomy results in 45 chromosomes in each cell.
Trisomy - an EXTRA copy of a chromosome, resulting in 47 instead of 46 chromosomes.
Meiosis failure - Most cases of simple aneuploidy usually due to meiotic non-disjunctions (Meiosis separation issues)

Karyotype
Karyotype or karyogram - a display or photomicrograph of an individual’s  somatic-cell metaphase chromosomes that are  arranged in a standard sequence (usually based on number, size, and type)
Karyotype -  A complete set of chromosomes in an individual’s cells. It covers chromosome sizes, numbers, and shapes.

slides.text:
How Do Scientists Identify Chromosomes?
Three key features to identify their similarities  and differences:

Size - Easiest way to tell two different  chromosomes apart.

Banding pattern - The size and location of Giemsa bands (G-Bands) on chromosomes. 

Centromere position - Centromeres are regions in chromosomes that appear as a constriction.

Using these key features, scientists match up the  23 pairs of chromosomes.

Classification of chromosomal anomalies
Number of chromosomes affected (usually due to error in meiosis)
Aneuploidy - The presence of an abnormal number of chromosomes in a cell.

Polyploidy – The presence of more than one pair of (homologous) chromosomes.

Rearrangement of chromosomes (structural issues ; may be due to error in meiosis or inherited)
Translocations - Unusual rearrangement of chromosomes.   
Deletions -  parts of chromosomes are missing, chromosome deletion syndrome
Duplications -  Chromosome duplication disorders occur due to errors in cell division.
Inversions - An inversion is a chromosome rearrangement in which a segment of a chromosome becomes inverted within its original position.

slides.topic: Chromosomal Abnormalities I — Karyotypes & Numerical Disorders — source 57
slides.text:
Dosage Compensation
Dosage - levels of gene activity produced by a single X chromosome is the normal "dosage" for a human. 

Men - Have this dosage because they only have one X chromosome! 

Women - Have the same dosage for a different reason: they shut down one of their two X chromosomes in a process called X-inactivation.

X-inactivation - an X chromosome is compacted ("crumpled up into a ball"), to make a small, dense structure called a Barr body. Most of the genes on the Barr body are inactive, meaning that they are not transcribed. 

Mary Lyon - The process of X-inactivation was discovered by the British geneticist Mary F. Lyon. The Lyon hypothesis, after Mary Lyon, who  first proposed in 1962.

slides.topic: Chromosomal Abnormalities I — Karyotypes & Numerical Disorders — source 58
slides.text:
Female Mammals Are Mosaics
X inactivation - once occurred in a cell, it is  permanent in all the descendants of that cell.

Mosaic - All female mammals are mosaic for the genes on the X chromosome because of the random inactivation of one or the other X chromosome in all their somatic cells.

Female mammals are mosaics of two populations of cells; one expresses the maternal X and the  other the paternal X

Alleles of both chromosomes are expressed approximately equally over the whole organism
